definition: The practice of dividing a dataset into separate subsets for training a model and evaluating its performance on unseen data.
details: A proper train-test split (often supplemented with a validation set) is essential for producing an honest estimate of how well a model will generalize to new, unseen data.

explainer.lead: A train-test split divides a dataset into separate subsets for training a model and evaluating it on unseen data. It matters because it produces an honest estimate of how well a model will generalise.

tiers.eli5: It's like studying with practice questions but being graded on different ones, so you know you actually learned the material.
tiers.practitioner: Engineers hold out a test subset, often adding a validation set for tuning, and evaluate only once on the held-out data. A common pitfall is leakage between splits or tuning repeatedly on the test set, which inflates the reported performance.
tiers.paperLevel: Formally, a dataset D is partitioned into disjoint training and test subsets; the model is fitted on the training subset and its generalisation is estimated from performance on the test subset. The estimate is only honest if the test subset is truly unseen and not reused for model selection.

explainer.example: An 80/20 split trains on 8,000 examples and reports accuracy on the remaining 2,000, which the model never saw during fitting.
